overview.text: An earthquake is ground shaking caused when rocks suddenly slip along a fault, a break between blocks of Earth’s crust. Tectonic plates move slowly, but friction can hold fault edges in place; stress then builds until the rocks slip, releasing energy that travels outward as seismic waves. This process is described by elastic-rebound theory. Earthquakes matter because their waves shake the ground and can damage buildings. Magnitude describes an earthquake’s size, while shaking intensity can vary from place to place. Some undersea earthquakes also shift the seafloor and generate tsunamis, but this requires particular conditions and does not happen with every earthquake.

key_facts.text: Fault edges can stick because of friction as tectonic plates move; when built-up stress overcomes friction, the sudden slip releases energy as seismic waves.
Elastic-rebound theory describes how rocks gradually store stress and then release it suddenly when a fault slips.
Magnitude describes an earthquake’s size; intensity describes shaking at particular locations and can differ across the affected area.
The Richter scale is not commonly used for most earthquakes today; USGS says moment magnitude is a more accurate measure for those events.
Some undersea earthquakes can generate tsunamis by moving the seafloor, but not every earthquake does so.
